entries.name: Atlantic herring
entries.migrates: seasonal migrations between offshore feeding banks and coastal spawning grounds
behaviour: forms dense schooling ribbons km wide
broadcasts adhesive eggs over gravel banks
the single most important forage fish of the north Atlantic

voxel_model.pattern: blue-green back, silvery flanks, dark shoulder spot

entries.notes: The shimmering staple of northern seas; one of the most numerous vertebrates on Earth. Historic fisheries collapsed and recovered more than once — a clean model for fishery collapse mechanics.

entries.name: Peruvian anchoveta
entries.migrates: shifts with the Humboldt current; collapses catastrophically during El Niño
behaviour: the largest single-species fishery on Earth by tonnage
powers vast seabird and sea-lion colonies on the Peru coast
crashes almost completely when warm El Niño water replaces cold nutrient-rich upwelling

voxel_model.pattern: steel blue back, silver flank, bluish stripe

entries.notes: The engine of Peru's upwelling coast, harvested for fishmeal and fertilizer. El Niño years are the classic case of one climate flip cascading through a whole ecosystem.

entries.name: Atlantic mackerel
entries.migrates: seasonal north-south movements along the shelf edge, overwintering in the deep
behaviour: shoots through the water in fast direct bursts, no loitering
schools by the hundreds of thousands offshore
a favourite of anglers and of everything that eats fish

voxel_model.pattern: iridescent blue-green with dark wavy vertical bars

entries.notes: The striped boxer of the cool Atlantic; fat, fast and unbothered. Excellent mid-tier fishing-game prey: common enough to matter, quick enough to miss.

entries.name: Harbor porpoise
entries.migrates: mostly resident, with coastal seasonal shifts in some populations
behaviour: the smallest, shiest cetacean in the northern hemisphere
swims with a distinctive low cruising motion and rarely breaches
navigation and hunting by high-frequency clicks

voxel_model.pattern: dark grey back and pale white belly, blunt head

entries.notes: The shy coastal porpoise: no beak, no splash, just a low grey crescent and a blow. Protected across its range; in the game, an ambient wildlife encounter, not a hunt.

entries.name: Vaquita
behaviour: smallest cetacean on Earth; lives only in the northern Gulf of California
decline driven almost entirely by bycatch in illegal totoaba gillnets
fewer than ten individuals are thought to remain

voxel_model.pattern: grey back, white belly, dark rings around eyes and lips

entries.notes: The porpoise on the edge of extinction: so few remain that every model is a memorial. A content warning and a conservation-sign post rather than a spawnable animal.

entries.name: Tropical two-wing flyingfish
behaviour: launches out of the water and glides on enlarged pectoral fins
glides of 200 m or more at speeds near 60 km/h
its eggs are sticky balls lodged onto floating seaweed and debris

voxel_model.pattern: dark blue back, silver belly, sail-like pectoral wings

entries.notes: The two-winged rocket of the tropics: an underwater predator chase turns into a low skimming missile over the swell. A perfect dramatic encounter on any warm-water crossing.

entries.name: Lumpfish
behaviour: a walking, suction-disc fish: its pelvic fins form an adhesive organ
females are harvested for their roe, sold as lumpfish caviar
farmed in salmon pens as a living sea-lice cleaner

voxel_model.pattern: mottled grey-brown, knobbly back, sucker belly

entries.notes: The dumpy button of cold seas with a genuinely useful job: it hoovers sea lice off farmed salmon and its roe stocks cocktail platters. An aquaculture-oddity drops entry.

entries.name: Stoplight parrotfish
behaviour: scrapes algae off coral rock with fused beak-like teeth
excretes coral skeleton as brilliant white sand — a single fish passes hundreds of kilograms a year
sleeps inside a self-made mucus cocoon that masks its scent

voxel_model.pattern: green body, red stern, pale scale edges, red beak

entries.notes: The reef's gardener and sand factory: reefs are quite literally grown out of parrotfish droppings. Male territories sparkle — ideal visual anchor for a coral biome.

entries.name: Regal tang
behaviour: famously blue with black palette-shaped markings
carries a razor-sharp caudal spine ('scalpel') erected when threatened
iconic of coral reefs and of the aquarium trade

voxel_model.pattern: royal blue body, black artist-palette motif, yellow tail

entries.notes: Dory, in the flesh: a piece of swimming iconography. Popular as a pet, hard to breed in captivity, so wild-caught pressure is a real threat — a natural aquarium-trade hook.

entries.name: Bluestreak cleaner wrasse
behaviour: runs an open-air cleaning station: larger fish queue up and hold still
cleans predators including moray eels and sharks without being eaten
cheats sometimes take a bite of client mucus — clients remember the cheats

voxel_model.pattern: black stripes lengthwise on iridescent blue

entries.notes: The reef's dentist: a tiny wrasse that negotiates with great white sharks for a living. Cleaning stations are ready-made set-pieces for any reef encounter.

entries.name: Red lionfish
entries.migrates: invasive spread across the Atlantic since the 1900s
behaviour: fan of venomous dorsal spines used purely for defence
invaded the Atlantic from abandoned aquariums; devastates reef fish stocks
corners prey with sweeping pectoral fins and a gape that doubles its mouth

voxel_model.pattern: vertical rust and cream stripes, fan of long spines

entries.notes: Beautiful, armed and everywhere: the lionfish is the Atlantic's poster child for invasive species. In the game, catching one to save the reef is an obvious questline.

entries.name: Olive sea snake
behaviour: evolved from Australian land snakes, fully aquatic and unable to move on land
breathes partly through its skin while submerged
venom potent but bites are rare and reluctant

voxel_model.pattern: olive green body, yellow-olive belly, paddle tail

entries.notes: A land snake that gave up the land: perfectly aquatic, harmless unless grabbed. Touching reef life carelessly invites one — keep it a watch-out, not a weapon.

entries.name: Atlantic mudskipper
behaviour: a fish that lives out of water, breathing through skin and mouth lining
walks on muscular pectoral fins across tidal mudflats
digs burrows it retreats to at high tide

voxel_model.pattern: mottled brown, pale speckles, raised eyes like periscopes

entries.notes: The fish on stilts: it hunts insects and crabs on mudflats with its eyes on top of its head. Muddy shorelines are not empty — the mudskipper is the payoff.

entries.name: Common octopus
behaviour: unscrews jars, uses tools, learns mazes — the gold standard of invertebrate intelligence
females guard eggs for weeks, then starve to death
crawls on the seabed; jets only in emergencies

voxel_model.pattern: mottled orange-brown, colour-shifting on distress

entries.notes: The problem-solving cephalopod of every warm coast; it dies after one brood, every time. Treasure-hunter encounter: it answers observation with experiment.

entries.name: Common cuttlefish
entries.migrates: seasonal inshore migrations to warm spawning shallows in spring
behaviour: changes colour, pattern and texture in under a second via millions of chromatophores
rival males display battle Halloweens of pulsing stripes at females
its internal cuttlebone gives neutral buoyancy and litters beaches

voxel_model.pattern: banded zebra pulsing through browns, greys and white

entries.notes: The camouflage artist in chief: it can out-dazzle a video screen. Cuttlebones on beaches are the breadcrumb trail for any observant player.

entries.name: Peacock mantis shrimp
behaviour: strikes prey with club appendages accelerating like a .22 calibre bullet, cavitation bubble included
16 photoreceptor classes vs 3 in humans, including circularly polarised light
smashes crab and snail shells like an armored wrecking ball

voxel_model.pattern: electric blue, orange, green and magenta, hard-edged blocks

entries.notes: The army of the small: it smashes glass and bone at 23 m/s of acceleration. Absolutely the creature a glass-blowing player never wants loose in an aquarium.

entries.name: Blue mussel
behaviour: threads itself to rock with byssus silks stronger than steel by weight
farmed by the million tonnes; filters a bay clean
clusters intertidally, half in air at every low tide

voxel_model.pattern: dark blue-black shell, hint of purple

entries.notes: The supermarket shellfish and the tidepool classic; it sticks to everything. Farmed lines of mussels are a great coastal structure for a lived-in world.

entries.name: Pacific oyster
behaviour: cultivated worldwide for food; the default 'oyster' of farms
builds jagged reef clusters that shelter hundreds of species
a single adult filters up to 200 litres of water a day

voxel_model.pattern: whitish-cream, rough-foliated grey-brown crust

entries.notes: The farm gate of coastal food: reef-building ecosystem engineer on the one hand, cash crop on the other. Oyster pearls as the rare lucky drop.

entries.name: Great scallop
behaviour: jets away by clapping its shells, snapping like castanets
rimmed with a hundred tiny blue eyes that detect motion and light
the shell of pilgrims and the emblem of Santiago de Compostela

voxel_model.pattern: reddish-pink fan with radiating ribs, creamy interior

entries.notes: The pilgrim's fan with 60-plus eyes: it sees you coming and swims away. A scalloper sweep is the ocean's most elegant escape mechanic.

entries.name: Horseshoe crab
entries.migrates: moves inshore onto beaches to spawn under spring high tides
behaviour: a 450-million-year-old living fossil, unchanged since before trees
copper-based blue blood is harvested to test every injectable drug for bacterial toxins
aggregates by the thousands on Delaware Bay beaches to spawn

voxel_model.pattern: domed rust-brown helmet shell, long spike tail

entries.notes: The drug-safety horseshoe: every vaccine on Earth was once screened by its blue blood. Delaware Bay spawning is one of the great coastal spectacles.

entries.name: Common hermit crab
behaviour: moves into empty mollusc shells and abandons them when it outgrows them
forms vacancy chains: dozens line up to trade shells in sequence
waggles a shell-antenna at neighbours in shell negotiations

voxel_model.pattern: red-orange legs, cream-banded, off-white shell

entries.notes: The tidepool diplomat: shells are scarce currency and he knows the market rate. The vacancy-chain trade is a wonderful small AI emergent behaviour.

entries.name: Acorn barnacle
behaviour: glues its head to the rock head-down and kicks food into its mouth with feathered legs
waves feeding fans at high tide, clamps shut at low tide
Darwin's namesake obsession: he spent years classifying barnacles

voxel_model.pattern: white-grey volcano cone with 6 wall plates

entries.notes: The volcano that feeds: every wave-washed rock groans with these. A tidepool game needs it — it's the background noise of the upper shore.

entries.name: Purple sea urchin
behaviour: grazes kelp with five-toothed jaw called Aristotle's lantern
when kelp vanishes it starves into a self-mummifying 'zombie urchin' state
urchin barrens replace kelp forests when otters disappear

voxel_model.pattern: deep purple spines over a dark violet test

entries.notes: The kelp-forest famine: without otters, these turn forests into purple deserts. Uni lovers harvest the gonads; marine-biology types grieve the barrens.

entries.name: Geography cone snail
behaviour: fires a hollow radular harpoon loaded with paralysing venom at fish
one of the most venomous animals on the planet; no antivenom exists
engulfs small fish whole, sometimes still flapping as it swallows

voxel_model.pattern: cream cone marbled with chestnut streaks

entries.notes: The land-mine of the tropics: beautiful, slow, and absolutely not to be picked up by beachcombers. A signpost animal: pretty shell, wrong hands, bad day.

entries.name: By-the-wind sailor
entries.migrates: drifts with the wind; thousands wash ashore together after onshore gales
behaviour: not a jellyfish but a floating colony of polyps, distant man o' war relative
its chitin sail catches the wind at a constant 40-degree angle
windrows of blue sails carpet beaches after spring storms

voxel_model.pattern: deep cobalt oval float with a translucent sail fin

entries.notes: The blue confetti of stormy spring beaches: strand by the thousand, harmless, eerily beautiful. Natural weather flag for a coastal world.

entries.name: Beadlet sea anemone
behaviour: clamps shut into a red blob when poked, tentacles and all
wages stinging-acrorhagi wars with neighbouring anemones over rock
a true battery of microscopic stinging harpoons, all spring-loaded

voxel_model.pattern: blood-red column, darker tentacles

entries.notes: The tidepool traffic cone: every British rockpool has one and every child has poked one. Ideal permanent resident of any rocky shore.

entries.name: Sea gooseberry
behaviour: an eight-row comb jelly: cilia beat in waves that scatter a rainbow shimmer
retracts its two long tentacles into side slots when threatened
blooms explosively in nutrient-rich, fished-out or warm waters

voxel_model.pattern: ghostly clear orb rippling with rainbow bands

entries.notes: The rainbow-ripple ghost of the plankton: harmless, hypnotic, and a bloom-warning sign. Perfect as a translucent ambient shimmer in sheltered bays.

entries.name: Orange sea cucumber
behaviour: waves five pairs of feathery tentacles into the current to trap plankton
draws them one by one through its mouth like mopping a counter
close cousin of bêche-de-mer, the dried-cucumber delicacy of Asia

voxel_model.pattern: burnt orange body with darker tentacle feathers

entries.notes: The seafloor's slow feather-duster: odd, calm, and commercially valuable in dried form. A quiet crafting ingredient for a well-travelled chef.

entries.name: Christmas tree worm
behaviour: lives cemented inside a coral tube it grows alongside the coral
its twin spiral crown of radioles unfurls to feed and snaps shut in a blink
lives longer than most fish on the same reef

voxel_model.pattern: paired candy-bright spirals, blue, red, yellow or green

entries.notes: The reef's living Christmas decorations: colour you never forget once you spot them zipping shut. Ideal collectible for a reef-crawl achievement.

entries.name: Common fangtooth
entries.migrates: daily vertical migration from abyssal 5,000 m to within 50 m of the surface
behaviour: proportionally the largest teeth of any fish — they do not fit inside its mouth otherwise
hauls itself up the water column each night to hunt
distributed in every deep ocean, essentially a global citizen of the abyss

voxel_model.pattern: almost black, rough scaled plates, knife jaw

entries.notes: The abyss's toothache: fangs that make it look like a nightmare, in a fish barely longer than your finger. Deep-water horror flavour for any trench.

entries.name: Barreleye
entries.migrates: stays between 600 and 800 m depth, drifting
behaviour: inside its transparent fluid-filled dome sit two barrel-shaped green eyes that swivel
the dome likely shields the eyes from siphonophore stings
first observed alive by ROV in 2004

voxel_model.pattern: dark body under a clear dome, greenish eye-tubes

entries.notes: The fish behind glass: a 1990s sci-fi concept delivered by evolution. An ROV-only encounter — most players will only ever see the skeleton.

entries.name: Northern lanternfish
entries.migrates: migrates hundreds of metres up at dusk and back down at dawn, daily
behaviour: photophores along belly and sides erase its silhouette from below (counter-illumination)
one of the single most abundant fishes on the planet by biomass
the deep scattering layer of sonar is largely lanternfish

voxel_model.pattern: silvery belly, dark back, rows of glowing dots

entries.notes: The hidden biomass colossus: migrate it nightly in your game and the sky goes white with predators. Lanternfish literally carry the deep sound layer.

entries.name: Calanoid copepod
entries.migrates: daily vertical migration; some populations overwinter at depth
behaviour: the master currency of the northern food web
stores thick wax-ester ballast that survives winter starvation
responsible for most of the spring phytoplankton crash when it hatches

voxel_model.pattern: transparent orange-red teardrop with red eye spot

entries.notes: The atom of the north Atlantic food web: you cannot overate this. Render it as shimmering plankton clouds, never as individuals.

entries.name: Sea angel
entries.migrates: forms immense polar and subpolar swarms
behaviour: flaps wing-like parapodia in slow graceful beats through freezing water
launches six buccal hooks to seize sea butterflies inside their shells
floats entirely translucent — nearly invisible when still

voxel_model.pattern: fully translucent amber-white, faint gut line

entries.notes: The polar angel: beautiful, glassy, armed. It eats sea butterflies — the two make a tidy ecology lesson for a cold-water level.

entries.name: Sea butterfly
entries.migrates: dense polar swarms, sometimes turning whole bays lilac
behaviour: an armoured pteropod with two flapping 'wings' over a coiled shell
first casualty of ocean acidification: its argonite shell dissolves in CO2-rich water
a key food of seabirds, whales and salmon larvae

voxel_model.pattern: translucent spiral shell, soft golden wings

entries.notes: The canary in the acidified coal mine: its thinning shell is the headline of ocean chemistry. Vanish it from the food web and everything above starves.

entries.name: Firefly squid
behaviour: covered in photophores: three arm-tip dots glow laser-blue
spring nights in Toyama Bay see millions wash ashore in a blue fire
lives 200-600 m deep by day, rising at dusk to hunt

voxel_model.pattern: dark violet body freckled with glowing cyan dots

entries.notes: The natural light show: the only fishing light people travel to see. In-game, a rare spring night event worth a whole questline.

entries.name: Vampire squid
behaviour: neither vampire nor squid, but a tiny folding cloak of doom
eats drifting organic debris — the only cephalopod that filters
its eyes are the largest relative to body size of any animal

voxel_model.pattern: velvety black-purple cloak, webbed arms, ice-blue eyes

entries.notes: The abyss that came dressed as a demon and turned out to be a polite vegetarian. Best served as a rare deep-sea find that lowers nothing's heart rate.

entries.name: Greater blue-ringed octopus
behaviour: wears the most famous warning labels in the ocean: electric blue rings on yellow
saliva carries tetrodotoxin; a bite paralyses, then stops breathing
mothers guard eggs, then die; males starve themselves during courtship

voxel_model.pattern: yellow-brown with vivid blue rings edged in black

entries.notes: The golf-ball that kills: do not pick up tidepool octopuses. A perfect tutorial on colour as language — bright is biologically serious.

entries.name: Blue dragon sea slug
entries.migrates: drifts inverted on the sea surface, pushed by wind and current
behaviour: floats upside-down beneath the surface film, belly to the sky
harvests stinging nematocysts from its venomous prey and stores them on its back
delivers concentrated nukes back at predators

voxel_model.pattern: vivid azure finger-winged body, silver-blue belly

entries.notes: The sea's klepto-predator: it eats the man o' war and wears its stolen venom like armour. Do not step on it either — the stolen sting still works.

entries.name: Spanish dancer
behaviour: swims by undulating its body in big crimped waves, like a flamenco skirt
one of the largest nudibranchs alive, bright red-orange warning colour
pairs hunt same sponges in ritual courtship trains

voxel_model.pattern: brilliant vermilion with black-tipped white gill tufts

entries.notes: The flamenco of the reef: a half-metre slug that flies like a living banner. Night divers pay money to see one mid-glide.
